Place `counts.csv` and `meta_data.csv` beside this document before
knitting. The supplied download names `counts(1).csv` and
`meta_data(1).csv` are also accepted. The count file must have gene IDs
in its first column and sample IDs as the remaining column names. The
metadata must contain one row per sample. Install dependencies once in
the Console, then knit in a clean R session.

## 1. Setup and reusable functions

```{r setup}
# Course guide: Lecture 1: Functions; Lecture 2: Packages and summary statistics.
# Install packages in the Console once; do not install while knitting.
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "stringr", "tibble", "ggplot2",
#                    "data.table", "knitr", "circlize"))
# install.packages("BiocManager")
# BiocManager::install("ComplexHeatmap")
# Check all direct dependencies before starting the analysis.
pkg_need <- c("dplyr", "tidyr", "stringr", "tibble", "ggplot2",
              "data.table", "knitr", "kableExtra", "circlize", "ComplexHeatmap")
pkg_miss <- pkg_need[!vapply(pkg_need, requireNamespace, logical(1),
                           quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(pkg_miss)) {
  stop("Install required packages before knitting: ",
       paste(pkg_miss, collapse = ", "))
}
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
library(ComplexHeatmap)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.keep = "all", fig.show = "asis",
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 300
)

# Use a portable figure destination for every export.
figure_dir <- function() {
  path <- file.path(getwd(), "figures")
  dir.create(path, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  if (!dir.exists(path)) stop("Could not create the Dartmouth figures folder.")
  normalizePath(path, mustWork = TRUE)
}
fig_dir <- figure_dir()
cat("Figure output folder:", fig_dir, "\n")

# Export each plot immediately so later chunks do not delay its files.
save_plot <- function(plot, name) {
  fig_dir <- figure_dir()
  ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, paste0(name, ".pdf")),
         plot = plot, width = 7, height = 4.5, units = "in", bg = "white")
  ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, paste0(name, ".png")),
         plot = plot, width = 7, height = 4.5, units = "in",
         dpi = 300, bg = "white")
}

# Close each heatmap device after drawing, including when an error occurs.
save_heatmap <- function(hm, name, format) {
  fig_dir <- figure_dir()
  path <- file.path(fig_dir, paste0(name, ".", format))
  if (format == "pdf") {
    pdf(path, width = 11, height = 6)
  } else {
    png(path, width = 11, height = 6, units = "in", res = 300,
        bg = "white")
  }
  on.exit(dev.off(), add = TRUE)
  ComplexHeatmap::draw(hm, merge_legends = TRUE)
}

# Use one theme so titles, labels, and borders remain consistent.
plot_theme <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(
        fill = "white", color = "lightgray", linewidth = 0.5
      ),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
      axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
    )
}

# Named colors keep the same group color across plots and annotations.
plot_col <- "blue"
type_col <- c(
  "Primary Tumor" = "#0072B2",
  "Solid Tissue Normal" = "#009E73",
  "Metastatic" = "#D55E00"
)
sub_col <- c(
  "Basal" = "#0072B2", "Her2" = "#D55E00", "LumA" = "#009E73",
  "LumB" = "#CC79A7", "Normal" = "#E69F00"
)

 # UPDATED function for final
# Reuse one summary function for pooled and grouped counts.
# Return NA for statistics when no observed values are available.
count_summary <- function(val) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(val), all(is.na(val) | is.finite(val)))

  obs <- val[!is.na(val)]
  n <- length(obs)

  tibble::tibble(
    # Sample size and completeness
    n_samp = length(val),
    n_obs  = n,
    n_miss = sum(is.na(val)),
    pct_miss = if (length(val)) 100 * mean(is.na(val)) else NA_real_,

    # Central tendency
    mean   = if (n) mean(obs) else NA_real_,
    median = if (n) median(obs) else NA_real_,

    # Variation
    sd    = if (n > 1) sd(obs) else NA_real_,
    var   = if (n > 1) var(obs) else NA_real_,
    iqr   = if (n) IQR(obs) else NA_real_,

    # Distribution
    min = if (n) min(obs) else NA_real_,
    q1  = if (n) unname(quantile(obs, 0.25)) else NA_real_,
    q3  = if (n) unname(quantile(obs, 0.75)) else NA_real_,
    max = if (n) max(obs) else NA_real_,

    # Standard error
    se = if (n > 1) sd(obs) / sqrt(n) else NA_real_
  )
}




# Validate a small extracted count matrix before any numeric coercion.
# This avoids turning unexpected text into silent missing values.
check_counts <- function(dat) {
  if (!all(vapply(dat, is.numeric, logical(1)))) {
    stop("Selected count columns must be numeric; inspect counts.csv.")
  }
  mat <- as.matrix(dat)
  if (any(!is.na(mat) & (!is.finite(mat) | mat < 0))) {
    stop("Selected counts must be nonnegative and finite, or NA.")
  }
  mat
}

# Ensembl lookup: require one row per gene and retain original IDs.
match_genes <- function(panel, ids, src_ids) {
  n_hit <- vapply(panel$ens_id, function(id) sum(ids == id, na.rm = TRUE), integer(1))
  if (any(n_hit != 1L)) {
    stop("Missing or ambiguous gene rows: ",
         paste(panel$gene[n_hit != 1L], collapse = ", "))
  }
  panel %>% mutate(idx = match(ens_id, ids), src_id = src_ids[idx])
}
```

These plots describe raw RNA-seq counts. Log transformation compresses
their range; it does not normalize library size. The heatmap displays
row z-scores of log10(count + 1), so its colors represent relative
variation within each gene. This script does not perform
differential-expression or paired interaction tests.

## 2. Load data

```{r load}
# Course guide: Lecture 2: Reading in Publicly Available Data.
# Read counts.csv and meta_data.csv from the folder containing this Rmd.
find_input <- function(candidates) {
  found <- candidates[file.exists(candidates)]
  if (!length(found)) {
    stop("Place an input CSV beside the Rmd: ",
         paste(candidates, collapse = " or "))
  }
  if (length(found) > 1L) {
    stop("Multiple input candidates found; retain one: ",
         paste(found, collapse = ", "))
  }
  found
}
cts_file <- find_input(c("counts.csv", "counts(1).csv"))
meta_file <- find_input(c("meta_data.csv", "meta_data(1).csv"))

cts <- data.table::fread(
  cts_file,
  data.table = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

meta <- data.table::fread(
  meta_file,
  data.table = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  colClasses = "character"
)

names(cts)[1] <- "gene_id"

# Verify required fields before selecting or renaming metadata columns.
meta_cols <- c("barcode", "patient", "sample_type", "ajcc_pathologic_stage",
               "paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50")
if (nrow(cts) == 0L || ncol(cts) < 2L ||
    !all(meta_cols %in% names(meta))) {
  stop("Check the count matrix dimensions and required metadata columns.")
}
if (anyNA(cts$gene_id) || any(trimws(cts$gene_id) == "")) {
  stop("The count matrix contains missing or blank gene IDs.")
}
```

## 3. Align samples

```{r align}
# Course guide: Lecture 2: Combine gene counts with metadata; Assignment 3, Q1: joins.
# Match metadata rows to count columns; never assume the original order.
samp_id <- names(cts)[-1]

stopifnot(
  "barcode" %in% names(meta),
  !anyNA(meta$barcode),
  all(nzchar(trimws(meta$barcode))),
  all(nzchar(trimws(samp_id))),
  !anyDuplicated(samp_id),
  !anyDuplicated(meta$barcode),
  setequal(samp_id, meta$barcode)
)

meta <- meta[match(samp_id, meta$barcode), , drop = FALSE]
rownames(meta) <- NULL

stopifnot(identical(samp_id, meta$barcode))
```

## 6. Review sample characteristics

```{r meta-review}
# Course guide: Lecture 2: Filter, select, and create variables; Assignment 3, Q1: recoding.
# Select descriptive fields and standardize missing category labels.
# Keep the original metadata unchanged.
meta_view <- meta %>%
  transmute(
    samp_id = barcode, pt_id = patient, type = sample_type,
    stage = ajcc_pathologic_stage, subtype = paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50
  )

# Clean descriptive labels without changing the source metadata.
na_val <- c("", "na", "n/a", "not reported", "unknown")
meta_view <- meta_view %>%
  mutate(across(c(type, stage, subtype), ~ {
    val <- str_trim(.x)
    replace(val, str_to_lower(val) %in% na_val, NA_character_)
  }))

# Reject unfamiliar labels before manual colors or factors can hide them.
if (any(!is.na(meta_view$type) & !meta_view$type %in% names(type_col)) ||
    any(!is.na(meta_view$subtype) &
        !meta_view$subtype %in% names(sub_col))) {
  stop("Unexpected tissue or subtype label; inspect metadata and palettes.")
}
meta_view$pt_id <- na_if(str_trim(meta_view$pt_id), "")

head(meta_view)

# Sample and patient totals.
n_samp <- nrow(meta_view)
n_pt <- n_distinct(meta_view$pt_id, na.rm = TRUE)

data.frame(n_samp, n_pt)

# Category counts, including missing values.
table(meta_view$type, useNA = "ifany")
table(meta_view$stage, useNA = "ifany")
table(meta_view$subtype, useNA = "ifany")

# Check how subtype labels are distributed across tissue types.
with(meta_view, table(type, subtype, useNA = "ifany"))
```

## 7. Define analysis groups

```{r groups}
# Course guide: Lecture 2: Adding and Removing Rows and Columns.
# Keep all samples for tissue analyses; define a primary-tumor subset.
# Confirm metadata still matches count-column order.
stopifnot(identical(names(cts)[-1], meta_view$samp_id))

# All samples remain available for tissue-type comparisons.
type_idx <- which(!is.na(meta_view$type))

# Primary tumors with a recorded subtype.
sub_idx <- which(
  meta_view$type == "Primary Tumor" &
  !is.na(meta_view$subtype)
)

if (!length(sub_idx)) {
  stop("No primary tumors have recorded subtypes; check metadata labels.")
}
sub_meta <- meta_view %>% slice(sub_idx)

# Summarize groups without copying the large count matrix.
data.frame(
  group = c("Known sample type", "Primary tumor with subtype"),
  n_samp = c(length(type_idx), length(sub_idx))
)

table(sub_meta$subtype)

# Later, use sub_idx to select count columns.
# Add 1 because the first column contains gene IDs:
# cts[gene_idx, sub_idx + 1L, drop = FALSE]
```

## 8. Summarize PAM50 subtype counts

```{r subtype-table}
# Course guide: Lecture 2: Summarize & count by group.
# Report observed PAM50 subtype counts and percentages.
# Reuse sub_meta from the preceding chunk.
sub_tab <- sub_meta %>%
  count(subtype, name = "n_samp") %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n_samp / sum(n_samp), 1))

knitr::kable(
  sub_tab,
  col.names = c("Subtype", "Samples", "Percent (%)"),
  digits = 1,
  caption = paste0(
    "Primary tumors with a recorded subtype (n = ",
    format(nrow(sub_meta), big.mark = ","),
    ")."
  )
)
```

Primary tumors without a recorded PAM50 subtype are retained in
tissue-type analyses and excluded only from subtype analyses.



## 9. Select genes

```{r gene-select}
# Course guide: Assignment 1, Q2: gene selection; Lecture 2: String Manipulation.
# Identify ESR1 and ERBB2 using stable Ensembl identifiers.
gene_sel <- tibble(
  gene = c("ESR1", "ERBB2"),
  ens_id = c("ENSG00000091831", "ENSG00000141736")
)

# Remove version suffixes only in a separate lookup vector.
gene_id <- sub("\\.[0-9]+$", "", cts$gene_id)

gene_sel <- match_genes(gene_sel, gene_id, cts$gene_id)
gene_idx <- gene_sel$idx

gene_sel
```

## 10. Extract gene counts

```{r gene-counts}
# Course guide: Lecture 2: Extract gene counts and combine them with metadata.
# Build a small plotting table without pivoting the entire count matrix.
stopifnot(identical(names(cts)[-1], meta_view$samp_id))

# Extract only two rows from the large matrix, then use tidyverse downstream.
gene_ct <- check_counts(cts[gene_idx, -1, drop = FALSE])
gene_dat <- meta_view %>%
  mutate(
    ESR1 = as.numeric(gene_ct[1, ]),
    ERBB2 = as.numeric(gene_ct[2, ])
  )

# Fail clearly rather than plotting malformed count data.
stopifnot(
  all(is.na(gene_dat$ESR1) | (is.finite(gene_dat$ESR1) & gene_dat$ESR1 >= 0)),
  all(is.na(gene_dat$ERBB2) | (is.finite(gene_dat$ERBB2) & gene_dat$ERBB2 >= 0))
)

head(gene_dat)

# Primary tumors with recorded subtypes.
sub_dat <- gene_dat %>% slice(sub_idx)

stopifnot(nrow(sub_dat) == nrow(sub_meta))
```


## 11. ESR1 and ERBB2 summary statistics

```{r gene-summary}
# Course guide: Lecture 2: Generating Summary Statistics.
# Summarize raw gene counts and report missingness.
# FINAL TABLE DISPLAYING SUMMARY STATS FOR TWO GENES, UPDATED 
gene_sum <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  count_summary(gene_dat$ESR1) %>%
    mutate(gene = "ESR1", .before = 1),

  count_summary(gene_dat$ERBB2) %>%
    mutate(gene = "ERBB2", .before = 1)

# Present selected descriptive statistics
knitr::kable(
  gene_sum %>%
    select(
      gene, n_obs, n_miss,

    ),

  booktabs = TRUE,

  format.args = list(

  ),

  ),

```


## 12. ESR1 count distribution


```{r esr1-hist, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5, results='asis'}
# Course guide: Assignment 1, Q2; Lecture 3.
# Log2 visualization with raw-count descriptive statistics.
# Final updates, log2, mean, median, and quartiles, and skewness check on org data.
# Center The Graph around Mean
esr1_stats <- gene_sum %>%
  filter(gene == "ESR1")

# Original observations and transformed display values
esr1_raw <- na.omit(gene_dat$ESR1)
esr1_x <- log2(esr1_raw + 1)

# Center the x-axis around the raw-count mean
esr1_mean_x <- log2(esr1_stats$mean + 1)

half_span <- max(abs(esr1_x - esr1_mean_x)) * 1.05

p_hist <- ggplot(
  gene_dat %>% drop_na(ESR1),
  aes(x = log2(ESR1 + 1))
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 40,
    fill = plot_col,
    color = "white"
  ) +

  # Mean
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = esr1_mean_x,
    color = "firebrick",
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +

  # Median
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = log2(esr1_stats$median + 1),
    color = "navy",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +

  # First and third quartiles
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = log2(
      c(esr1_stats$q1, esr1_stats$q3) + 1
    ),
    color = "darkgreen",
    linetype = "dotted",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +

  # Symmetric plotting limits around the mean
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(
      esr1_mean_x - half_span,
      esr1_mean_x + half_span
    ),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +

  labs(
    title = "Distribution of ESR1 counts",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Log2-transformed raw counts | n =",
      length(esr1_raw)
    ),
    x = "log2(ESR1 raw count + 1)",
    y = "Number of samples",
    caption = paste(
      "Red = Raw-count mean | Blue = Median |",
      "Green = Q1 and Q3"
    )
  ) +
  plot_theme()

print(p_hist)
save_plot(p_hist, "esr1_histogram")


# Skewness of original, untransformed ESR1 counts
#This is a check to make sure we are describing our skewness correctly
esr1_skew <- if (length(esr1_raw) > 2 && sd(esr1_raw) > 0) {
  mean((esr1_raw - mean(esr1_raw))^3) /
    sd(esr1_raw)^3 *
    (length(esr1_raw) / (length(esr1_raw) - 1))^(3/2)
} else NA_real_

# Classify original distribution
shape <- if (is.na(esr1_skew)) {
  "could not be classified"
} else if (esr1_skew > 0.5) {
  "skewed to the right (positive skew)"
} else if (esr1_skew < -0.5) {
  "skewed to the left (negative skew)"
} else {
  "approximately symmetric"
}

# Research interpretation
cat(
  "\n\n**Distribution interpretation:**",
  "The original ESR1 raw-count distribution is", shape,
  sprintf("(skewness = %.2f).", esr1_skew),
  "\n\n"
)
```


## 13. ESR1 and ERBB2 comparison

```{r gene-scatter, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
# Course guide: Lecture 3: scatter plots; Assignment 2, Q3(c): scatter plot.
# Compare two genes on clearly labeled log10(count + 1) axes.
#Update: added in regression, with CI interval and p value. made little display on top

# Prepare complete observations
scatter_dat <- gene_dat %>%
  drop_na(ESR1, ERBB2)

# Fit linear regression on the log10 scale
reg_model <- lm(
  log10(ERBB2 + 1) ~ log10(ESR1 + 1),
  data = scatter_dat
)

# Extract regression statistics
reg_sum <- summary(reg_model)

b0 <- coef(reg_model)[1]
b1 <- coef(reg_model)[2]
r2 <- reg_sum$r.squared
p_val <- reg_sum$coefficients[2, 4]

# Format p-value
p_label <- if (p_val < 0.001) {
  "p < 0.001"
} else {
  sprintf("p = %.3f", p_val)
}

# Regression annotation
reg_label <- sprintf(
  "y = %.2f %s %.2fx\nR² = %.3f\n%s",
  b0,
  ifelse(b1 < 0, "-", "+"),
  abs(b1),
  r2,
  p_label
)

# Scatter plot
p_scat <- ggplot(
  scatter_dat,
  aes(x = log10(ESR1 + 1), y = log10(ERBB2 + 1))
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.4,
    size = 1.5,
    color = plot_col
  ) +

  # Linear regression with 95% confidence interval
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = TRUE,
    level = 0.95,
    color = "firebrick",
    fill = "grey",
    linewidth = 0.9,
    linetype = "solid"
  ) +

  # Regression equation and statistics
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = Inf,
    y = Inf,
    label = reg_label,
    hjust = 1.05,
    vjust = 1.15,
    size = 3.5,
    fill = "white",
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +

  labs(
    title = "ESR1 and ERBB2 counts",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Both genes observed: n =", nrow(scatter_dat)
    ),
    x = "ESR1: log10(raw count + 1)",
    y = "ERBB2: log10(raw count + 1)",
    caption = paste(
      "Red line = Linear regression |",
      "Shaded region = 95% confidence interval"
    )
  ) +
  plot_theme()

print(p_scat)
save_plot(p_scat, "gene_scatter")

```

This graph is exploratory, and should considered as such, as this is a representation of counts. Counts or observations are expected, when dealing with similar sampling. This could potentially be something noted for further analysis.

```{r esr1-violin, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
    alpha = 0.5,
    trim = TRUE,
    color = "grey10"
  ) +

  # Individual samples
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0.12,
    height = 0,
    alpha = 0.25,
    size = 0.8,
    color = "grey10"
  ) +

  # Median and interquartile range
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    fill = "white",
    color = "grey10",
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +

  scale_fill_manual(values = type_col) +

  labs(
    title = "ESR1 expression by tissue type",
    subtitle = "Distribution of observed RNA-seq raw counts",
    x = "Tissue type",
    y = "log10(ESR1 raw count + 1)",
    caption = paste(
      "Points: Individual samples  |",
      "Box: Median and IQR  |",
      "Violin: Estimated density"
    )
  ) +

  plot_theme() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "grey40",
      hjust = 0.5
    )
  )

print(p_vln)
save_plot(p_vln, "esr1_sample_type")

```

This graph tells us that we have a very small sampling of metastatic patient corpora to work with, about 7. Early detection for metastatic cancer through machine learning will have a difficult time with such a small sample size. We also note that we have a decent sampling of primary tumor, along side normal tumor. The violin plot here is used to examine the data counts we are working with, to establish a mental reference for future analysis. 

## 15. ESR1 by primary-tumor subtype

```{r esr1-subtype, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
# Course guide: Lecture 2: grouped gene-count plots; Assignment 3, Q2(a): violin plot.
# Compare primary tumors by their recorded PAM50 subtype.
# Updated the violin segment here as well, primarly for the jitter points, viewabliltiy

# So pretty simple math, we are going to take a look at the outliers, 
# and then just give them a white dot, to view them better. 

# Prepare ESR1 observations and identify outliers
sub_plot <- sub_dat %>%
  drop_na(subtype, ESR1) %>%
  mutate(ESR1_log = log10(ESR1 + 1)) %>%
  group_by(subtype) %>%
  mutate(
    q1 = quantile(ESR1_log, 0.25),
    q3 = quantile(ESR1_log, 0.75),
    is_outlier = ESR1_log < q1 - 1.5 * (q3 - q1) |
                 ESR1_log > q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# ESR1 distribution by PAM50 subtype
p_sub <- ggplot(
  sub_plot,
  aes(x = subtype, y = ESR1_log, fill = subtype)
) +

  # Distribution density
  geom_violin(
    alpha = 0.5,
    trim = TRUE,
    color = "grey10"
  ) +

  # Individual observations
  geom_jitter(
    data = filter(sub_plot, !is_outlier),
    width = 0.12,
    height = 0,
    alpha = 0.25,
    size = 0.8,
    color = "grey5"
  ) +

  # Median and interquartile range
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    fill = "white",
    color = "grey10",
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +

  
  # Paul's Note's - Research guide
  # Outliers: white circles with dark borders
  
  geom_jitter(
    data = filter(sub_plot, is_outlier),
    width = 0.12,
    height = 0,
    shape = 21,
    fill = "white",
    color = "grey10",
    stroke = 0.5,
    size = 1.6,
    alpha = 1
  ) +

  scale_fill_manual(values = sub_col) +

  labs(
    title = "ESR1 expression by recorded PAM50 subtype",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Labeled primary tumors with ESR1 counts: n =",
      nrow(sub_plot)
    ),
    x = "Recorded PAM50 subtype",
    y = "log10(ESR1 raw count + 1)",
    caption = paste0(
      "Dark points: Observations | White points: Outliers (1.5 x IQR)\n",
      "Box: Median and IQR | Violin: Estimated density\n",
      sum(
        meta_view$type == "Primary Tumor" &
        is.na(meta_view$subtype),
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
      " primary tumors excluded for missing subtype labels."
    )
  ) +

  plot_theme() +
  theme(
    # Light grey background
    panel.background = element_rect(
      fill = "grey94", color = NA
    ),
    plot.background = element_rect(
      fill = "grey94", color = NA
    ),

    # Subtle horizontal gridlines
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "white",
      linewidth = 0.5
    ),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),

    # Clean presentation
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "grey20",
      hjust = 0.5
    )
  )

print(p_sub)
save_plot(p_sub, "esr1_subtype")


```

In reviewing plot creation the color scale can be applied to the colors directly after the name, which is a great way to get exactly the shade you are looking for. It's handy when you forget how to do it, then remember it, because it makes the points look presentable to peers. The white outlier is a nice addition that took a little bit to config. It highlights visually the outliers for the user to see them on a latex print out. It's more presentable this way, along with documenting the exclusions, with re:.

## 16a. Export LaTeX tables

Final output preparation: export tables for inclusion in the LaTeX manuscript. This chunk let's us easily export the tables, and then just import them automatically into laxteX when every they compile, making our lives easier. I use a standard select call, as always, then just work the function. 

```{r export-latex-tables, echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
# ============================================================
# Export TCGA-BRCA tables directly to LaTeX
# Requires: sub_tab, gene_sum, sub_sum
# ============================================================



# Save tables to the existing figures/output directory
table_dir <- fig_dir
dir.create(table_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Reusable export function
export_tex_table <- function(data, filename, caption, columns) {

  latex <- knitr::kable(
    data,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    caption = caption,
    col.names = columns,
    digits = 1,
    format.args = list(
      big.mark = ",",
      scientific = FALSE
    )
  )

  writeLines(latex, file.path(table_dir, filename))
}

# Table 1: PAM50 subtype distribution
export_tex_table(
  sub_tab %>% select(subtype, n_samp, pct),
  "pam50_distribution.tex",
  "PAM50 molecular subtype distribution among primary tumors.",
  c("Subtype", "Samples", "Percent (%)")
)

# Table 2: ESR1 and ERBB2 descriptive statistics
export_tex_table(
  gene_sum %>%
    select(gene, n_obs, n_miss, mean, median, sd, iqr, min, max),
  "gene_summary.tex",
  "ESR1 and ERBB2 raw-count descriptive statistics.",
  c("Gene", "N", "Missing", "Mean", "Median",
    "SD", "IQR", "Min", "Max")
)

# Table 3: ESR1 statistics by PAM50 subtype
export_tex_table(
  sub_sum %>%
    select(subtype, n_obs, mean, median, sd, iqr, min, max),
  "esr1_by_subtype.tex",
  "ESR1 raw-count statistics by PAM50 molecular subtype.",
  c("Subtype", "N", "Mean", "Median",
    "SD", "IQR", "Min", "Max")
)

# Verify exported files
table_files <- file.path(
  table_dir,
  c(
    "pam50_distribution.tex",
    "gene_summary.tex",
    "esr1_by_subtype.tex"
  )
)

stopifnot(
  all(file.exists(table_files)),
  all(file.info(table_files)$size > 0)
)

cat("LaTeX tables exported successfully:\n")
cat(paste(table_files, collapse = "\n"))
```

## 18. Prepare the heatmap matrix

```{r heatmap-data}
# Course guide: Lecture 1: matrices and transpose; Lecture 3: Heatmaps.
# Log-transform selected counts and standardize each gene across samples.
stopifnot(identical(names(cts)[-1], meta_view$samp_id))

# Rows are genes; columns are samples.
hm_ct <- check_counts(cts[hm_idx, -1, drop = FALSE])
rownames(hm_ct) <- hm_genes$gene

stopifnot(
  is.numeric(hm_ct),
  all(is.finite(hm_ct)),
  all(hm_ct >= 0)
)

# Compress the count range, then standardize each gene across samples.
hm_log <- log10(hm_ct + 1)
hm_sd <- apply(hm_log, 1, sd)

if (any(!is.finite(hm_sd) | hm_sd == 0)) {
  stop("A selected gene has no usable variation.")
}

hm_z <- t(scale(t(hm_log)))

# Match annotation rows explicitly to matrix columns.
hm_meta <- meta_view[
  match(colnames(hm_z), meta_view$samp_id),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

stopifnot(identical(colnames(hm_z), hm_meta$samp_id))

# Retain samples with missing tissue labels as an explicit heatmap slice.
hm_type <- factor(
  replace_na(hm_meta$type, "Missing"),
  levels = c(names(type_col), "Missing")
)
```

## 19. Draw the annotated heatmap

```{r heatmap-plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=6}
# Course guide: Lecture 3: Heatmaps, annotations and clustering.
# Cluster selected genes and samples; annotate tissue and subtype.
# Pauls' Notes Heat map best practices
# R Heatmap guide https://r-graph-gallery.com/heatmap 
# Econometrics homework 2025 Z scores reference



# -----------------------------------------------
# Heatmap annotations
# -----------------------------------------------

# Top annotation: tissue type and PAM50 subtype
hm_ann <- HeatmapAnnotation(
  Type = hm_type,
  Subtype = hm_meta$subtype,
  col = list(
    Type = c(type_col, "Missing" = "#D9D9D9"),
    Subtype = sub_col
  ),
  na_col = "#D9D9D9",
  annotation_name_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 9)
)

# rowmeans against the high low 
# Side annotation: low and high standardized expression
z_pct <- cbind(
  "Low"  = 100 * rowMeans(hm_z < -1, na.rm = TRUE),
  "High" = 100 * rowMeans(hm_z >  1, na.rm = TRUE)
)

hm_side <- rowAnnotation(
  "Z-score tails (%)" = anno_barplot(
    z_pct,
    beside = TRUE,
    gp = grid::gpar(
      fill = c("#2166AC", "#B2182B"),
      col = NA
    ),
    border = FALSE,
    width = grid::unit(2.5, "cm"),
    axis_param = list(
      gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 8)
    )
  ),
  annotation_name_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 9)
)


# -----------------------------------------------
# Heatmap construction
# -----------------------------------------------

hm <- Heatmap(
  hm_z,
  name = "Row z-score",

  # Expression color scale
  col = circlize::colorRamp2(
    c(-2, 0, 2),
    c("#2166AC", "#FFFFFF", "#B2182B")
  ),

  # Annotations
  top_annotation = hm_ann,
  right_annotation = hm_side,

  # Sample grouping
  column_split = hm_type,
  column_title = NULL,
  cluster_column_slices = FALSE,

  # Hierarchical clustering
  cluster_columns = TRUE,
  cluster_rows = TRUE,
  clustering_distance_rows = "euclidean",
  clustering_distance_columns = "euclidean",
  clustering_method_rows = "complete",
  clustering_method_columns = "complete",

  # Presentation
  show_column_names = FALSE,
  show_column_dend = FALSE,
  row_names_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 10),
  use_raster = FALSE
)

# -----------------------------------------------
# Display and export
# -----------------------------------------------

# Legend for the side annotation
tail_legend <- ComplexHeatmap::Legend(
  title = "Z-score tails",
  at = c("Z < -1", "Z > +1"),
  legend_gp = grid::gpar(
    fill = c("#2166AC", "#B2182B")
  ),
  title_gp = grid::gpar(
    fontsize = 10,
    fontface = "bold"
  ),
  labels_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 9)
)

# Consistent rendering with all legends
draw_gene_heatmap <- function() {
  ComplexHeatmap::draw(
    hm,
    merge_legends = TRUE,
    annotation_legend_list = list(tail_legend)
  )
}

# Display in report
draw_gene_heatmap()

# Export PDF
grDevices::pdf(
  file.path(fig_dir, "gene_heatmap.pdf"),
  width = 14,
  height = 8
)
draw_gene_heatmap()
invisible(grDevices::dev.off())

# Export PNG
grDevices::png(
  file.path(fig_dir, "gene_heatmap.png"),
  width = 2800,
  height = 1600,
  res = 200
)
draw_gene_heatmap()
invisible(grDevices::dev.off())

# Verify exported files
stopifnot(
  file.exists(file.path(fig_dir, "gene_heatmap.pdf")),
  file.exists(file.path(fig_dir, "gene_heatmap.png"))
)
#DO i EXIST?

```

So for expanding my heat map I went with taking a gander at the z-score tails. I first did just a z score, which came out poorly. Then i broke it up into pos and neg scores. This gave me the viewing perspective I was looking for. I wanted to look at FOXA1 because it looked off relative to the others in this sample batch. It warrants further investigation into it's nature. It would be nice to have a larger sample for metastatic for this type of heat map, however; we work with what we have. For references I used my notes I made on paul's notes github, the R-graph-gallery, and I needed to reference my notes from 2025 on z-scores from my econometrics work for the code chunk I was specifically looking to reference. (rowmeans against the high low)


## 20. Exploratory volcano-style plot

```{r gene-volcano, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
# Course guide: Lecture 3, scatterplots and scientific visualization.
# Instructional DISPLAY ONLY: this is NOT a differential-expression analysis.
# Contrast: Primary Tumor versus Solid Tissue Normal.


# Match existing metadata to the original count columns.
stopifnot(identical(names(cts)[-1], meta_view$samp_id))
vol_idx <- which(meta_view$type %in% c("Primary Tumor", "Solid Tissue Normal"))
vol_tumor <- meta_view$type[vol_idx] == "Primary Tumor"
stopifnot(sum(vol_tumor) >= 3, sum(!vol_tumor) >= 3)

# Keep the demonstration manageable: a fixed sample of genes plus
# the ten markers used in the heatmap. No fabricated measurements.
set.seed(711)
vol_rows <- unique(c(
  hm_idx,
  sample.int(nrow(cts), min(3000L, nrow(cts)))
))

vol_ct <- as.matrix(cts[vol_rows, vol_idx + 1L, drop = FALSE])
stopifnot(is.numeric(vol_ct), all(is.finite(vol_ct)), all(vol_ct >= 0))

# Total counts across ALL genes set each sample's library-size denominator.
vol_lib <- vapply(cts[-1], function(x) sum(x, na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(vol_lib[vol_idx]) & vol_lib[vol_idx] > 0))

# Limit the display to genes with at least 10 counts in 10 samples.
vol_keep <- rowSums(vol_ct >= 10) >= 10
vol_ct <- vol_ct[vol_keep, , drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(nrow(vol_ct) >= 2)

# Simple counts-per-million adjustment for visualization (NOT DESeq2).
vol_cpm <- sweep(vol_ct, 2, vol_lib[vol_idx] / 1e6, "/")
vol_log <- log2(vol_cpm + 1)

# Illustrative log2 ratio of mean CPM values, with a +1 pseudocount.
vol_fc <- log2(
  (rowMeans(vol_cpm[, vol_tumor, drop = FALSE]) + 1) /
  (rowMeans(vol_cpm[, !vol_tumor, drop = FALSE]) + 1)
)

# Simple Welch tests for teaching the visual; repeated people, batch,
# and RNA-seq count-dispersion are NOT modeled here.
vol_p <- apply(vol_log, 1, function(x) {
  tryCatch(
    t.test(x[vol_tumor], x[!vol_tumor])$p.value,
    error = function(e) NA_real_
  )
})

vol_dat <- tibble(
  gene_id = cts$gene_id[vol_rows[vol_keep]],
  gene = hm_genes$gene[match(vol_rows[vol_keep], hm_idx)],
  log2FC = vol_fc,
  padj = p.adjust(vol_p, method = "BH")
) %>%
  drop_na(log2FC, padj) %>%
  mutate(
    neg_log10_padj = pmin(-log10(pmax(padj, .Machine$double.xmin)), 20),
    status = case_when(
      padj < 0.05 & log2FC <= -1 ~ "Lower",
      padj < 0.05 & log2FC >= 1 ~ "Higher",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )
stopifnot(nrow(vol_dat) > 0)

vol_xlim <- max(2, ceiling(max(abs(vol_dat$log2FC))))

p_vol <- ggplot(vol_dat, aes(x = log2FC, y = neg_log10_padj)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = status), alpha = 0.6, size = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    data = vol_dat %>% filter(!is.na(gene)),
    aes(label = gene),
    size = 2.8, vjust = -0.7, check_overlap = TRUE,
    color = "grey10"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Lower" = "#2166AC", "Other" = "grey65",
               "Higher" = "#B2182B"),
    breaks = c("Lower", "Other", "Higher"),
    labels = c("Lower in tumor", "Other", "Higher in tumor"),
    name = "Illustrative cutoff"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-vol_xlim, vol_xlim)) +
  labs(
    title = "Exploratory volcano-style display",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Primary Tumor vs Solid Tissue Normal | Genes shown:", nrow(vol_dat)
    ),
    x = "Log2 ratio of mean CPM (+1 pseudocount)",
    y = "-log10(BH-adjusted Welch p-value)",
    caption = paste(
      "Dashed: |log2 ratio| = 1; BH p = 0.05 | Y capped at 20.\n",
      "Instructional-only; does not account for pairing, batch or count dispersion."
    )
  ) +
  plot_theme() +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "grey94", color = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "grey94", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8, color = "grey30", hjust = 0.5)
  )

print(p_vol)
save_plot(p_vol, "gene_volcano")
```

### Exploratory analysis notes

Subtype labels are supplied metadata, not newly inferred PAM50
classifications. Samples can include multiple tissues from the same
patient; descriptive plots alone do not account for that pairing. These
figures summarize expression patterns and provide a starting point for
further analysis. Take with a grain of salt, the data is exploratory.
